id: Love Poem So Tall It Ends in Heaven

prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

A man I loved kept a folded square of masking tape in his pocket He did this / only for a year His masking tape was bright orange and fraying As evidence / coroners had used it to attach to his father’s calf the rope his father’d used / This man planted the tape in our yard when the year was done and from it grew thirteen beams / From these beams rafters grew Ropes uncurled from these rafters and fathers hanged from the ropes / Over the fathers a roof blossomed like a shield and against it a ladder leaned / The ladder was so tall the man I loved said it must have ended in heaven And down / from the ladder an angel scurried while we slept In its mouth it carried torn strips / of tape The angel pressed this tape on the calves of the man I loved like bandages / Each morning I removed the tape I was careful not to wake him Each morning / he’d walk through the garden of swaying fathers He’d kneel beside our rosemary bush / He’d rub its leaves in his hands He’d ball his hands in his hair to scent it He wanted / just to keep his earthliness with him / In hell this is the only prerequisite

prompts.L3:
Please expand the following bullet points into a complete, well-structured text:

- A man carried a fraying square of orange masking tape that coroners had used as evidence after his father’s suicide.
- After a year, he buried the tape in the yard, where it grew into a nightmarish structure of beams, rafters, ropes, and hanging fathers.

outputs.L2:
For one year only, someone I loved carried a small piece of masking tape, doubled over, inside his pocket. It was vivid orange, its edges worn to threads. The coroner had once used it as a label, fastening to his father’s lower leg the rope with which his father had died.

When the year ended, he buried the tape in our garden. Thirteen wooden supports rose from that spot, sprouting crosspieces above them. From those timbers, ropes loosened themselves, and from every rope a father hung.

A roof opened over their bodies, flowering into protection. A ladder rested against it, so impossibly high that the man I loved believed its top reached heaven. While we were asleep, an angel hurried down its rungs, carrying scraps of torn tape between its teeth. It laid the strips across his calves as though dressing wounds.

At daybreak, I peeled them away gently so he would not stir. Every morning, he passed through the garden where the suspended fathers rocked. Beside our rosemary plant, he dropped to his knees, crushed its leaves between his palms, then tangled his hands in his hair to leave their fragrance there. He wished to preserve some trace of being earthly.

That is all hell requires.
outputs.L3:
For a year, the man carried a fraying square of orange masking tape that the coroners had collected as evidence after his father’s suicide. The tape became a private relic, worn soft at the edges by his touch, as though it still held some trace of the room, the body, or the life that had ended there.

At last, he buried it in the yard. But the tape did not decay. Instead, it took root and grew into a nightmarish structure of beams and rafters, crowded with ropes and the hanging bodies of fathers. A roof slowly formed above them, and against it leaned an immense ladder that seemed to rise beyond the world and reach all the way to heaven.

Each night, an angel descended the ladder. Kneeling beside the man, it wrapped his calves in strips torn from the buried tape. Each morning, the speaker removed those bandages, undoing the angel’s work before daylight could make it permanent.

To keep himself bound to earthly life, the man crushed rosemary between his palms and rubbed its scent into his hands and hair. That lingering fragrance—sharp, green, and mortal—preserved his connection to the living world, a connection described as the sole prerequisite for hell.
outputs.L4:
The poem explores inherited trauma, grief, and suicide through a sequence of surreal, unsettling transformations. At its center is the image of a dead father’s evidence tape being planted in the earth. The gesture resembles both burial and cultivation: something associated with death, investigation, and violence is treated like a seed. Yet what grows from it is not a source of ordinary renewal. Instead, it becomes a house-like garden made of ropes, rafters, and hanging fathers. Domestic space, natural space, and the scene of death collapse into one another, suggesting that trauma cannot be contained in the past. It takes root in the family’s inner life and reproduces itself across generations.

The repeated image of the father is especially significant. Rather than appearing as a single lost individual, he seems to multiply, turning private grief into a larger inheritance. The “hanging fathers” may represent memory’s compulsive return to the moment of death, but they also evoke the fear that suffering passes from parent to child. The house, which should offer shelter and continuity, becomes inseparable from the means of suicide. Ropes and rafters are both structural and threatening: they hold the imagined house together while also recalling the violence that destroyed the family. In this way, the poem shows how bereavement can alter the meaning of familiar objects until the whole world appears organized around loss.

The poem’s surrealism gives form to an experience that cannot be expressed adequately through literal description. Planting evidence tape is impossible, just as a garden cannot naturally grow fathers, yet these impossibilities communicate the logic of traumatic memory. Grief does not move neatly from pain toward resolution. It spreads, repeats, and transforms, making the dead simultaneously absent and inescapably present. The imagery also blurs agency: it is unclear whether the speaker is trying to preserve the father, understand his death, or bury its evidence. That uncertainty reflects the bereaved person’s impossible desire both to remember and to escape what remembrance continually revives.

Against these violent images, the poem introduces recurring angelic bandages and rosemary. Bandages imply care, tenderness, and the attempt to heal, but they also acknowledge that a wound exists and may never fully close. Their angelic quality gives acts of care a spiritual dimension without presenting them as miraculous cures. Love can wrap the injury, protect it, and make survival possible, but it cannot undo the death or erase the suffering that preceded it. The poem therefore resists easy consolation. Its angels do not rescue the speaker from grief; they accompany the speaker within it.

Rosemary likewise carries associations of remembrance, mourning, and ritual. As a living herb, it offers a gentler form of growth than the terrible garden of ropes and rafters. It suggests that memory can be cultivated without allowing trauma to become the only thing that survives. Ritual does not solve grief, but it gives grief a shape: the dead can be named, mourned, and carried forward through repeated gestures of attention. Rosemary thus represents a form of fidelity to the father that does not require the speaker to repeat his destruction.

Ultimately, the poem presents survival not as transcendence but as the preservation of “earthliness.” This earthliness includes the body, ordinary affection, memory, care, and the stubborn continuation of life. To endure hell is not necessarily to escape suffering or discover a redemptive explanation for it. It is to remain human while passing through it. The angelic bandages and rosemary help the bereaved retain that humanity, even when love proves unable to save the dead. By placing fragile rituals of care beside images of inherited violence, the poem suggests that grief may never disappear, but it need not strip the living of their capacity for tenderness.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal prose poem about loving a man haunted by his father’s suicide, using orange masking tape, ropes, rafters, a ladder, an angel, and rosemary as recurring images.
counterfactuals.output:
I loved a man whose house remembered before he did.

In every room, orange masking tape marked the borders of invisible doors: one across the mirror, one around the telephone, one bright strip on the floor beneath the rafters. His father had left no map, only a ladder leaning into silence and a rope of questions no hand could untie.

At night, the rafters lowered like dark eyebrows. The ladder grew another rung. An angel sat on the highest step, smelling of dust and rosemary, and would not tell us whether it had come too early or too late.

I planted rosemary in cups along the windowsill. For remembrance, I said. For cooking, he answered, though neither of us was hungry.

We learned to live among ropes. The clothesline. The bathrobe belt. The orange cord of the lamp. Each one became a sleeping animal we stepped around carefully. He taped them with orange masking tape, little suns fastened to their bodies, as if brightness could make them harmless.

Sometimes his father entered him through the rafters. I could hear the old grief pacing overhead, dragging the ladder from dream to dream. My beloved would wake with sawdust in his mouth and an angel’s feather clenched in his fist.

I washed his hands with rosemary water.

I said: You are not the room.  
I said: You are not the rope.  
I said: The ladder can also lead down.

But love is not an exorcism. Love is kneeling beneath the rafters while the house rehearses its thunder. Love is laying orange masking tape across the cracks—not pretending they are healed, only making them visible enough that no one falls through.

Years passed strangely. The angel grew older. The rosemary became a tree, its roots winding through the foundation, its branches lifting the roof. The ropes softened into vines. The ladder flowered, one white blossom on every rung.

Still, some evenings, his father’s absence hung its coat in the hall.

Then my beloved would take my hand and lead me outside. We would wrap orange tape around the rosemary stems, bright flags against forgetting. Above us, the rafters of the sky opened and opened.

The angel descended—not to save us, not to explain—but carrying the ladder on its back like a useless wing.

Together we laid it on the grass.

Together we watched the moon climb.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose an experimental elegy in one dense paragraph, marking line breaks with slashes. Let ordinary evidence from a coroner’s investigation grow into a nightmarish garden of fathers, and end with a striking statement about the prerequisite for hell.
counterfactuals.output: The coroner inventories the room: one blue cup, three aspirin, a stopped watch, dust stippled across the sill like mild weather / he measures the bruise, seals a black thread in glass, notes the half-moon of bread gone hard beside the bed / but under his lamp the evidence germinates—each fingerprint uncurls a root, each root clenches the jaw of a father / fathers rise from the carpet in dark suits, their pockets stuffed with rain, their mouths full of the names they never used for love / one father blooms antlers of hospital tubing, another bears small white teeth where the roses should be, another kneels to prune the shadow from a child / soon the room is all garden: belts hanging like vines, apologies opening their red throats, family photographs swarming with flies of silver / the dead lie quiet beneath this inheritance while the living water it with questions / and the coroner, ankle-deep in paternal lilies, writes cause unknown though every flower has confessed / remember: hell requires a father to plant it.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a dark magical-realist poem in which a man carries a fraying square of tape once attached to the rope his father used to hang himself. After he buries it, transform the object into a house, a ladder to heaven, and angelic bandages.
counterfactuals.output:
**Adhesive**

For twenty years he carried  
a fraying square of tape—  
the piece once fastened to the rope  
his father used to leave the world.

It slept behind his license,  
pale as an old moth’s wing,  
collecting lint, tobacco,  
the small black weather of his pockets.

Some nights it warmed against his heart.  
Some nights it tightened there.  
He dreamed the rope still knew his name  
and practiced in the rafters.

At last he buried the square  
beneath the pear tree,  
where roots worked blindly  
through the grammar of the dead.

By morning, a house stood there.

Its windows were sealed with moonlight.  
Its doors opened only inward.  
In every room his father’s absence  
sat quietly, wearing a different coat.

From the chimney rose a ladder—  
rung after silver rung—  
climbing beyond birds, beyond weather,  
toward a heaven with no visible floor.

He climbed until the earth  
became a dark coin below him,  
but found no father at the top,  
only angels tending an enormous wound.

Their wings were wrapped  
in strips of yellowed adhesive.  
Their shining hands unspooled  
bandages from the clouds.

They bound the sky where it had torn.  
They bound his wrists, his mouth, his sleep.  
They wrapped the empty place inside him  
without closing it.

At dawn he woke beneath the pear tree.  
The house was gone. The ladder, gone.  
White feathers clung to every branch  
like gauze after a storm.

And in the grave, the little square  
held fast to nothing—  
which was, at last,  
the only thing it had been asked to hold.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a lyrical, unsettling poem narrated by someone caring for a grieving lover. Include the lover scenting his hair with rosemary to preserve his “earthliness,” and conclude with the line “In hell this is the only prerequisite.”
counterfactuals.output:
At night I rinse the cups of silence  
you leave beside the bed,  
each one filmed with the dark  
your mouth cannot swallow.

I warm milk, fold linen,  
count the pale moths battering the lamp  
as if they, too, have lost someone  
and mistake the burning for a door.

You sit between my knees  
and scent my hair with rosemary  
to preserve my earthliness—  
thumbs trembling at my temples,  
green needles caught like little bones.

You say the dead are jealous of perfume,  
of salt, of skin that bruises when pressed.  
I let you breathe me in  
until my scalp aches with your remembering.

By morning, the house has shifted.  
The hallway lengthens under our feet.  
Behind every mirror, someone waits  
wearing the face you miss.

Still, I button your coat.  
Still, I spoon the ash from your dreams.  
Still, I lie down beside you  
and practice being warm.

Love, you whisper, as though confessing a crime.  
Love, I answer, keeping perfectly still.

In hell this is the only prerequisite.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a contemporary free-verse poem about inherited trauma and suicide, blending domestic tenderness with grotesque botanical imagery. Avoid rhyme, use long enjambed sentences, and replace conventional stanza breaks with forward slashes.
counterfactuals.output:
My mother folded the towels into small white doors  
and taught me never to ask what waited behind them, her hands moving softly  
as moths over the warm cotton while beneath her nails the family garden  
pushed up its blind roots, knuckled and wet, feeding on names  
we had agreed not to pronounce /  

At breakfast my father cut pears into moons and left the knife beside the plate,  
its quiet shine entering the room before anyone spoke, and I learned how tenderness  
could butter toast, could wipe a mouth with the corner of a sleeve,  
could also carry a darkness from body to body like black pollen  
lodged in the throat of a flower that opened only at night /  

There were relatives who disappeared without leaving, their coats still breathing  
in the hall closet, their cups holding pale rings on the table,  
and those who ended their lives became grafts in us, crooked branches  
bound beneath the skin, budding in bad seasons with teeth instead of petals,  
with little red tongues tasting the air for weather /  

I do not blame the dead, though sometimes I feel them tending me  
with their ruined instruments, loosening the soil around my heart, whispering  
that surrender is an heirloom, a key wrapped in linen,  
but I have begun returning their gifts unopened, setting them gently  
beside the compost where every terrible thing is asked to become something else /  

Tonight I wash the dishes while someone I love dries them,  
and between us the ordinary plates pass like pale, survivable planets,  
our fingers touching in the steam as outside the garden heaves  
its obscene green machinery through the dark, bulbs splitting, roots gnawing  
the jawbones of winter, each stem lifting its soft wound toward morning /  

I cannot promise the old vine will die in me, only that I will keep pruning  
with whatever mercy I can hold, that I will name the blade and put it down,  
that I will sit at the kitchen table when the black blossoms open  
and let another living hand cover mine until the hour loosens,  
until the house, still haunted, begins again to smell of bread.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
